What is the water cycle?

The water cycle, also called the hydrological cycle, is the continuous movement of water between the earth and the atmosphere. It has no beginning and no end — the same water has been circulating for millions of years. The main stages are: evaporation, where heat from the sun turns water from rivers, lakes and the ocean into vapour; transpiration, where plants release water vapour from their leaves; condensation, where the rising vapour cools and forms clouds; precipitation, where the water falls back as rain (or hail); and collection or run-off, where the water gathers in rivers like the Niger and Benue, soaks into the ground, and eventually returns to the sea. This cycle is why our rainy season refills the streams and boreholes we drink from.

What is evaporation and what makes it happen faster?

Evaporation is the process by which a liquid changes into a gas or vapour. Heat energy from the sun gives the water molecules enough energy to escape from the surface and rise into the air as invisible water vapour. You see the effect every day: wet clothes on the line dry because the water evaporates, and a puddle after rain disappears under the hot sun. Evaporation happens faster when: the temperature is higher (clothes dry faster at noon than in the evening), the wind is stronger (breeze carries the vapour away), the surface area is larger (spread-out clothes dry faster than bunched ones), and the humidity is lower (which is why clothes dry faster in harmattan than during heavy rainy-season days).

What is condensation? Give an everyday example.

Condensation is the opposite of evaporation: it is the process by which water vapour (a gas) cools down and changes back into liquid water. As water vapour rises high into the atmosphere, the air up there is much colder, so the vapour cools and turns into tiny water droplets that cluster around dust particles — millions of these droplets together form a cloud. Everyday examples you can observe right now: water droplets forming on the outside of a cold bottle of soft drink or a sachet of pure water taken from the freezer; mist on a bathroom mirror after a hot bath; and dew on grass and car windscreens early in the morning. In each case, warm moist air touched a cold surface and the vapour condensed into liquid.

What is precipitation?

Precipitation is the stage of the water cycle where water falls from the clouds back down to the earth's surface. Inside a cloud, tiny droplets keep joining together and growing heavier; when they become too heavy for the air to hold up, gravity pulls them down. In Nigeria, precipitation falls mainly as rain, and occasionally as hail — those small ice pellets that sometimes fall during heavy thunderstorms. In very cold countries it also falls as snow and sleet, which we do not experience here. Precipitation is the stage that matters most to farmers: the rains that begin around April in the south water the maize, yam and cassava, which is why the farming calendar follows the rainy season closely.

What is transpiration and how is it part of the water cycle?

Transpiration is the release of water vapour from plants into the atmosphere, mainly through tiny pores in their leaves called stomata. Here is the journey: a plant absorbs water from the soil through its roots, the water travels up the stem to the leaves, the plant uses some for photosynthesis, and the excess escapes through the stomata as vapour. This adds a large amount of moisture to the air — a single big tree can release hundreds of litres of water in a day, which is why the air feels cooler and fresher inside a forest or under a big mango tree. Transpiration matters in the water cycle because it works alongside evaporation to supply the vapour that forms clouds; scientists often combine the two and call it evapotranspiration.

Why is the water cycle important to us in Nigeria?

The water cycle is important for many reasons.

First, it supplies fresh water: rain refills our rivers, streams, lakes and the underground water that boreholes and wells draw from, giving us water to drink, cook and wash.
Second, it supports agriculture: most Nigerian farmers depend on rain-fed farming, so the cycle decides when they plant maize, rice, yam and millet.
Third, it generates electricity: rain fills dams like Kainji and Shiroro on the River Niger, whose water turns turbines for hydroelectric power.
Fourth, it regulates temperature and weather, bringing the cool relief of rainy-season showers.
Finally, it purifies water naturally, because evaporation leaves salt and dirt behind, which is why rain is fresh even though it came from salty ocean water.

How can I demonstrate the water cycle in the classroom?

Here is a simple experiment you can do with everyday materials. You need a kettle or pot of water, a heat source, and a cold metal plate or spoon.

Step 1: heat the water until it boils and you see steam rising — that steam represents EVAPORATION from rivers and oceans, with the fire acting as the sun.
Step 2: hold the cold plate a little above the steam, using a cloth to protect your hand.
Step 3: watch water droplets form on the underside of the plate — that is CONDENSATION, exactly how clouds form when vapour meets cold air high up.
Step 4: keep watching until the droplets grow heavy and drip down — that is PRECIPITATION, our rain.

Always let your teacher handle the heat source. In four minutes you have modelled the whole cycle!

Does the earth ever run out of water since we keep using it?

Excellent question! The total amount of water on earth never changes — the water cycle recycles the same water endlessly, so the water you drink today may once have flowed in the River Niger or floated as a cloud over the Atlantic centuries ago. However, this does not mean water can never be scarce. Only about 3% of the earth's water is fresh, and much of that is locked in ice, so the usable share is small. Fresh water can also become unavailable where it is polluted by refuse and chemicals, where rain fails and drought strikes (as in parts of the far north), or where too many people draw from one source. So while the earth does not run out of water overall, clean water in a particular place can absolutely run short — which is why we must protect our streams and never waste or pollute water.
